   • Some of Russia’s closest partners are taking a more confrontational tone with President Vladimir Putin as the costs of the Ukraine war mount.

   • The death of a newborn who had measles has inflamed a debate over vaccination , as federal, state and local officials disagree over how much the disease was to blame.

   • Former NFL sideline reporter Michele Tafoya is trying to turn a Minnesota Senate seat red , leaning on voter anger over a massive welfare-fraud scandal.

   • The Supreme Court cleared the way for political parties to buy television advertisements at special reduced rates in the lead-up to the midterm elections.

       3. FROM THE MARKETS   • American workers have slammed the brakes on switching jobs , as a “low hire, low fire” labor market leaves many wary of job hopping.

   • U.S. diesel prices hit a record $5.85 a gallon , posing a fresh challenge for President Trump ahead of the midterm elections.

READ IT HERE FIRST   She was caught in Jeffrey Epstein’s “cult.” Getting out took years.   Julia Molchanova was 22, living in Russia and spoke little English when she met Jeffrey Epstein on a trip to New York. He offered to help the aspiring designer enroll at the Fashion Institute of Technology. “That was the hook,” she says. Instead, Epstein sexually abused her, Molchanova says, and drew her into a world where he dictated what she wore, whom she spent time with and even how long her hair should be. Years later, she began pushing back. Khadeeja Safdar tells the story of how Molchanova became ensnared in Epstein’s world and eventually escaped . Now, crypto is losing some of its most loyal traders to prediction markets , where they’re betting on everything from soccer matches and elections to the Federal Reserve’s next interest-rate move. Many are the same individual traders who fueled crypto’s past rallies, but some say event-based contracts are easier to trade than trying to make sense of crypto’s boom-and-bust cycles, write Vicky Ge Huang and Krystal Hur.
